items.stem: In which state are the particles close together but free to move past each other?
items.answer: Liquid
items.markingKey: Liquid: close, random arrangement, can slide past each other.

items.stem: Explain, using the particle model, why a solid has a fixed shape.
items.answer: The particles are held in fixed positions in a regular arrangement by strong forces between them; they can only vibrate.
items.markingKey: strong forces / fixed positions [1]; only vibrate [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a liquid can flow but cannot easily be compressed.
items.answer: The particles can move past each other, so it flows, but they are already touching, so there is little space to squeeze them into.
items.markingKey: particles move past each other [1]; close together, no space [1] [2]

items.stem: Mercury melts at −39 °C and boils at 357 °C. What is its state at 25 °C?
items.answer: liquid
items.markingKey: 25 °C is between melting and boiling points: liquid.

items.stem: Melting and boiling points: iron 1538 °C and 2862 °C; paraffin wax 55 °C and 370 °C. State the state of each at 25 °C and describe the motion of the particles in each.
items.answer: Iron: solid; paraffin wax: solid. Solid: particles vibrate about fixed positions.
items.markingKey: state of each [2]; particle motion description [1] [3]

items.stem: Nitrogen melts at −210 °C and boils at −196 °C. (a) Explain what happens to the particles when the substance melts. (b) Explain why the gas can be compressed but the liquid cannot easily be.
items.answer: (a) They gain energy and vibrate more until they break free of fixed positions and can move past each other. (b) Gas has large spaces between particles; in the liquid they are touching.
items.markingKey: (a) They gain energy and vibrate more until they break free of fixed positions and can move past each other (1 mark per correct point, max 2) [2] (b) Gas has large spaces between particles [1]; in the liquid they are touching [1] [2]

items.stem: Which state has a fixed shape and a fixed volume?
items.answer: Solid
items.markingKey: Solid particles vibrate about fixed positions.

items.stem: Explain why a gas fills any container it is put into.
items.answer: The particles move randomly at high speed in all directions with negligible forces between them, so they spread out to fill all the space.
items.markingKey: random fast motion [1]; weak forces, spread out [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe the differences in the arrangement and motion of particles in a solid and a gas.
items.answer: Solid: close, regular arrangement, vibrate about fixed positions. Gas: far apart, random arrangement, move rapidly in random directions.
items.markingKey: arrangement contrast [1]; motion contrast [1] [2]

items.stem: Lead melts at 327 °C and boils at 1749 °C. What is its state at 1849 °C?
items.answer: gas
items.markingKey: 1849 °C is above the boiling point: gas.

items.stem: Bromine melts at −7 °C and boils at 59 °C. (a) State the state of bromine at −17 °C. (b) State the state of bromine at 69 °C. (c) Explain why the gas is much less dense than the liquid.
items.answer: (a) Solid. (b) Gas. (c) Gas particles are much further apart.
items.markingKey: (a) Solid [1] (b) Gas [1] (c) Gas particles are much further apart [1]

items.stem: Nitrogen melts at −210 °C and boils at −196 °C. (a) State the state of nitrogen at −220 °C. (b) Explain why the gas is much less dense than the liquid. (c) Explain why the gas can be compressed but the liquid cannot easily be.
items.answer: (a) Solid. (b) Gas particles are much further apart. (c) Gas has large spaces between particles; in the liquid they are touching.

items.stem: Mercury melts at −39 °C and boils at 357 °C. (a) State the state of mercury at −49 °C. (b) State the state of mercury at 367 °C. (c) Describe the arrangement and motion of the particles in the liquid state. (d) Explain why the gas is much less dense than the liquid.
items.answer: (a) Solid. (b) Gas. (c) Close together, irregular arrangement, moving past each other. (d) Gas particles are much further apart.

items.stem: Brownian motion of smoke particles seen under a microscope is …
items.answer: random, jerky movement
items.markingKey: Smoke particles move randomly as they are hit by air molecules.

items.stem: Explain why smoke particles in air move randomly.
items.answer: They are bombarded by many much smaller, fast-moving air molecules from all sides; at any instant the collisions are unbalanced, so the smoke particle is pushed in a random direction.
items.markingKey: collisions with air molecules [1]; unbalanced, random [1]; molecules small and fast [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain, in terms of particles, why the pressure of a gas increases when it is heated at constant volume.
items.answer: The particles gain kinetic energy and move faster, so they hit the walls more often and with more force; force per unit area increases.
items.markingKey: faster particles [1]; more frequent collisions [1]; harder collisions / more force [1] [3]

items.stem: Gas at a pressure of 120 kPa acts on the inside wall of a gas cylinder of area 0.2 m². Calculate the force exerted by the gas.
items.markingKey: F = pA = 120 000 × 0.2 = 24 000 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Gas particles colliding with a piston in a cylinder of gas of area 200 cm² exert a total force of 2400 N. Calculate the gas pressure in kPa and explain how the particles produce this force.
items.answer: 120 kPa; the particles collide with the surface and change momentum, exerting a force.
items.markingKey: A = 0.02 m² [1]; p = F/A = 120 kPa [1]; collisions with surface exert force [1] [3]

items.stem: A teacher demonstrates Brownian motion using pollen grains in water. (a) State what this tells us about air molecules. (b) Predict how the motion changes if the air is warmed, and explain.
items.answer: (a) They are very small and moving rapidly and randomly. (b) More vigorous: air molecules move faster, so collisions are harder.
items.markingKey: (a) They are very small and moving rapidly and randomly (1 mark per correct point, max 2) [2] (b) More vigorous [1]; air molecules move faster, so collisions are harder [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the Brownian motion of smaller smoke particles is more vigorous than that of larger ones.
items.answer: Smaller particles have less mass, so the unbalanced forces from collisions give them a larger acceleration.
items.markingKey: smaller mass [1]; larger effect of unbalanced collisions [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a balloon expands when more air is pumped into it.
items.answer: More particles inside mean more collisions per second with the inside wall, increasing pressure inside above the pressure outside, so the rubber stretches.
items.markingKey: more particles → more collisions [1]; pressure inside > outside [1] [2]

items.stem: Consider the air inside a car tyre on a hot day in Seoul. The air is heated at constant volume. Predict how the pressure changes and explain in terms of the particles.
items.answer: Pressure will increase: particles move faster, hitting the walls more often and with more force.
items.markingKey: prediction [1]; speed of particles [1]; collisions frequency/force [1] [3]

items.stem: Gas at a pressure of 250 kPa acts on a square panel of a sealed tank of area 0.02 m². Calculate the force exerted by the gas.
items.markingKey: F = pA = 250 000 × 0.02 = 5000 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Gas particles colliding with a square panel of a sealed tank of area 2000 cm² exert a total force of 24 000 N. Calculate the gas pressure in kPa and explain how the particles produce this force.

items.stem: Ana looks at a smoke cell through a microscope. (a) Describe what is seen through the microscope. (b) Explain why larger particles show less Brownian motion.

items.stem: For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, if the volume is halved, the pressure …
items.answer: doubles
items.markingKey: pV = constant: p ∝ 1/V.

items.stem: Explain, in terms of particles, why compressing a gas at constant temperature increases its pressure.
items.answer: The same number of particles are in a smaller volume, so they hit the walls more often per unit area; their speed is unchanged (constant temperature) but the collision rate increases.
items.markingKey: same particles, smaller volume [1]; more frequent collisions per unit area [1]; same speed at constant T [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why the gas should be compressed slowly in an experiment to test pV = constant.
items.answer: Compressing quickly does work on the gas and warms it; going slowly lets thermal energy escape so the temperature stays constant.
items.markingKey: fast compression heats gas [1]; slow keeps T constant [1] [2]

items.stem: Gas in a syringe sealed at the nozzle has a volume of 80 cm³ at a pressure of 120 kPa. The volume changes to 160 cm³ at constant temperature. Calculate the new pressure.
items.answer: 60 kPa
items.markingKey: p₂ = p₁V₁/V₂ = 120 × 80/160 = 60 kPa. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Gas in a syringe sealed at the nozzle has a volume of 40 cm³ at 101 kPa. It is compressed slowly at constant temperature until the pressure is 200 kPa. Calculate the new volume.
items.answer: 20.2 cm³

items.answer: (a) 403 kPa (b) 20.1 cm³ (c) pressure outside falls, so the gas particles push the bubble wall out until the pressure inside matches; the same particles spread over a larger volume.

items.stem: A sample of gas is warmed from 0 °C to 250 °C. (a) Convert 0 °C to kelvin. (b) State the temperature change in kelvin. (c) Calculate the ratio of the average kinetic energy of the particles at the higher temperature to that at the lower temperature.
items.markingKey: (a) 273 K [1] (b) 250 K [1] (c) ratio of kelvin temperatures (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1.92 [1] [2]

items.stem: How do the particles in a solid move?
options: They move randomly at high speed
They do not move at all
items.answer: They vibrate about fixed positions
items.markingKey: Strong forces hold them in a regular lattice.

items.stem: State which state(s) of matter can be compressed easily and explain this using the particle model.
items.answer: Gas: large spaces between particles.
items.markingKey: correct state(s) [1]; particle explanation [1] [2]

items.stem: Ethanol melts at −114 °C and boils at 78 °C. What is its state at 178 °C?
items.answer: gas
items.markingKey: 178 °C is above the boiling point: gas.

items.stem: Paraffin wax melts at 55 °C and boils at 370 °C. (a) State the state of paraffin wax at 380 °C. (b) Describe the arrangement and motion of the particles in the liquid state.
items.answer: (a) Gas. (b) Close together, irregular arrangement, moving past each other.
items.markingKey: (a) Gas [1] (b) Close together [1]; irregular arrangement, moving past each other [1] [2]

items.stem: Lead melts at 327 °C and boils at 1749 °C. (a) State the state of lead at 317 °C. (b) Explain what happens to the particles when the substance melts. (c) Explain why the gas can be compressed but the liquid cannot easily be.
items.answer: (a) Solid. (b) They gain energy and vibrate more until they break free of fixed positions and can move past each other. (c) Gas has large spaces between particles; in the liquid they are touching.
items.markingKey: (a) Solid [1] (b) They gain energy and vibrate more until they break free of fixed positions and can move past each other (1 mark per correct point, max 2) [2] (c) Gas has large spaces between particles [1]; in the liquid they are touching [1] [2]

items.stem: How does a gas exert a pressure on the walls of its container?
options: Its particles collide with the walls, exerting forces on them
Its particles repel the walls without touching
Its particles stick to the walls
Gravity pulls the gas onto the walls
items.answer: Its particles collide with the walls, exerting forces on them
items.markingKey: Pressure = total force of collisions per unit area.

items.stem: Consider the air inside a car tyre on a hot day in Santiago. The air is heated at constant volume. Predict how the pressure changes and explain in terms of the particles.
items.answer: Pressure will increase: particles move faster, hitting the walls more often and with more force.
items.markingKey: prediction [1]; speed of particles [1]; collisions frequency/force [1] [3]

items.stem: Gas at a pressure of 300 kPa acts on a square panel of a sealed tank of area 0.02 m². Work out the force exerted by the gas.
items.markingKey: F = pA = 300 000 × 0.02 = 6000 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Gas particles colliding with the end of a bicycle pump of area 100 cm² exert a total force of 1200 N. Calculate the gas pressure in kPa and explain how the particles produce this force.
items.answer: 120 kPa; the particles collide with the surface and change momentum, exerting a force.
items.markingKey: A = 0.01 m² [1]; p = F/A = 120 kPa [1]; collisions with surface exert force [1] [3]

items.stem: Sofia looks at a smoke cell through a microscope. (a) Describe what is seen through the microscope. (b) Explain what causes this motion. (c) State what this tells us about air molecules.
items.answer: (a) Bright specks (smoke particles) moving in a random, jerky way. (b) Random collisions from invisible, fast-moving air molecules. (c) They are very small and moving rapidly and randomly.
items.markingKey: (a) Bright specks (smoke particles) moving in a random [1]; jerky way [1] [2] (b) Random collisions from invisible [1]; fast-moving air molecules [1] [2] (c) They are very small and moving rapidly and randomly (1 mark per correct point, max 2) [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) State two quantities that must be kept constant for pV = constant to apply. (b) Which equation applies to a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature?
items.answer: (a) The temperature and the mass (amount) of gas. (b) p₁V₁ = p₂V₂
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) Boyle’s law: pV = constant.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why air bubbles released by a diver get bigger as they rise. (b) Explain why the gas should be compressed slowly in an experiment to test pV = constant.
items.answer: (a) The water pressure decreases as the bubble rises (less depth), so at roughly constant temperature its volume increases (pV = constant). (b) Compressing quickly does work on the gas and warms it; going slowly lets thermal energy escape so the temperature stays constant.
items.markingKey: (a) pressure decreases with smaller depth [1]; V increases as p decreases [1] [2] (b) fast compression heats gas [1]; slow keeps T constant [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why air bubbles released by a diver get bigger as they rise. (b) Explain, in terms of particles, why compressing a gas at constant temperature increases its pressure.
items.answer: (a) The water pressure decreases as the bubble rises (less depth), so at roughly constant temperature its volume increases (pV = constant). (b) The same number of particles are in a smaller volume, so they hit the walls more often per unit area; their speed is unchanged (constant temperature) but the collision rate increases.
items.markingKey: (a) pressure decreases with smaller depth [1]; V increases as p decreases [1] [2] (b) same particles, smaller volume [1]; more frequent collisions per unit area [1]; same speed at constant T [1] [3]

items.stem: Diego compresses air in a syringe at constant temperature: volume/cm³ = 20, 48, 60, 80; pressure/kPa = 180, 63.8, 60, 45. (a) Calculate pV for each reading. (b) Identify the reading that does not fit and suggest a cause. (c) State the conclusion.
items.answer: (a) pV ≈ 3600 for all except the reading at 48 cm³ (3060). (b) 48 cm³ reading – e.g. temperature changed (compressed too quickly) or misread gauge. (c) pV is constant: p is inversely proportional to V.
items.markingKey: (a) products calculated [1] (b) anomaly identified with cause [1] (c) inverse proportion [1] [3]

items.stem: Helium in a party balloon has a volume of 8 litres at a pressure of 101 kPa. The volume changes to 12 litres at constant temperature. Determine the new pressure.
items.answer: 67.3 kPa
items.markingKey: p₂ = p₁V₁/V₂ = 101 × 8/12 = 67.3 kPa. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A sealed syringe contains 120 cm³ of air at 120 kPa. The plunger is pushed in slowly at constant temperature. (a) Calculate the pressure when the volume is 60 cm³. (b) Sketch-describe the graph of p against V.
items.answer: (a) 240 kPa (b) A curve (hyperbola): p decreases as V increases, never touching the axes.
items.markingKey: (a) p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ (method/substitution) [1]; answer 240 kPa with unit [1] [2] (b) A curve (hyperbola) [1]; p decreases, as V increases, never touching the axes [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) A student says "a gas at 40 °C has twice the particle energy of the same gas at 20 °C". Explain why this is wrong. (b) Explain why there cannot be a temperature lower than absolute zero.
items.answer: (a) Average kinetic energy is proportional to the Kelvin temperature: 313 K vs 293 K, an increase of only about 7%. (b) At absolute zero the particles have their minimum possible kinetic energy; they cannot have less, so the temperature cannot fall further.
items.markingKey: (a) must use kelvin [1]; 313/293 ≈ 1.07 [1] [2] (b) minimum KE [1]; cannot be reduced [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why there cannot be a temperature lower than absolute zero. (b) Explain how the average speed of gas particles is related to temperature.
items.answer: (a) At absolute zero the particles have their minimum possible kinetic energy; they cannot have less, so the temperature cannot fall further. (b) Higher temperature means a higher average kinetic energy of the particles, so they move faster on average; the Kelvin temperature is proportional to the average kinetic energy.
items.markingKey: (a) minimum KE [1]; cannot be reduced [1] [2] (b) temperature ∝ average KE [1]; higher T faster particles [1] [2]

items.stem: The surface of a pan is 180 °C. Calculate the temperature in kelvin.
items.markingKey: T = 180 + 273 = 453 K. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A sample of gas is warmed from −40 °C to 100 °C. (a) Explain why scientists prefer the Kelvin scale when studying gases. (b) Calculate the ratio of the average kinetic energy of the particles at the higher temperature to that at the lower temperature.
items.answer: (a) Kelvin temperature is proportional to the average kinetic energy of particles and has no negative values. (b) 1.6
items.markingKey: (a) Kelvin temperature is proportional to the average kinetic energy of particles and has no negative values (1 mark per correct point, max 2) [2] (b) ratio of kelvin temperatures (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1.6 [1] [2]
